To glut something means to fill it far beyond what it needs or can handle — to flood it with an overwhelming excess until it is completely stuffed, saturated, or overwhelmed.

The key word here is excess. Glut is not about simply filling something. It is about overfilling it to the point where what has been added becomes a burden, a problem, or causes things to slow down, break down, or lose value.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To glut a market (or a place / a system)

This is the most common use. When you glut a market, you flood it with so much supply of something that the market cannot absorb it all. There is simply more of the thing available than people want or need. As a result, the excess sits unused, prices drop, and the whole system feels overwhelmed.

Examples:

  • Cheap imports glutted the domestic steel market, causing prices to collapse.
  • A record harvest glutted the grain market, leaving farmers unable to sell at a profit.
  • Streaming platforms have glutted the entertainment industry with content, making it hard for any single show to stand out.

In each case, the supply has been pushed so far beyond demand that the market is now drowning in it.

2. To glut oneself (or to glut an appetite / a desire)

Here, glut means to satisfy a craving, appetite, or desire so completely — and so excessively — that you tip over into a state of being overfull, weary, or even disgusted. You don't just satisfy yourself; you indulge yourself beyond the point of satisfaction.

Examples:

  • He glutted himself on rich food during the festival and felt ill for days afterward.
  • She glutted her curiosity by reading every book on the subject she could find.
  • The soldiers had glutted their desire for revenge and now felt only emptiness.

Notice that in all three examples, the satisfaction has gone too far. There is always a sense that the indulgence crossed a line — it became too much.

Glut almost always carries a negative or at least cautionary tone. It suggests that a limit has been crossed. Think of it as the difference between quenching your thirst and drinking until you feel sick. Glut lives on the "sick" side of that line.

When a market is glutted, it is not thriving — it is struggling under too much supply.
When a person gluttes themselves, they are not pleasantly full — they are overwhelmed, weary, or regretful.

You will very frequently encounter glut in the passive voice: "glutted with." This is one of the most natural ways the word appears.

  • The market is glutted with used cars.
  • The city was glutted with tourists.
  • Her mind was glutted with information after the all-day seminar.

"Glutted with" simply means: overwhelmed by an excess of something.
The Subtle but Important Distinction from Similar Words

• Fill → neutral. Just means to put things in until there is no more space.
  • Flood → emphasises the sudden, overwhelming rush of something.
  • Saturate → means to fill something so completely that nothing more can be absorbed.
  • Glut → specifically emphasises that the excess has become a problem — prices fall, pleasure turns to discomfort, or the system cannot function properly. It is excess that hurts.

To glut is to supply, fill, or indulge something so far beyond its capacity or need that the excess itself becomes the problem — whether that is a market drowning in oversupply or a person made sick by overindulgence.
